bio_edx.1.6.summary: The brain is part of the central nervous system and is made of billions of neurones. Different regions carry out different functions: the cerebral hemispheres (cerebrum) control voluntary movement, the senses, language, memory and conscious thought; the cerebellum controls balance, posture and the fine coordination of muscles; and the medulla oblongata controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate. This content is for separate science Biology (triple) only.

core.h: Who needs this and where it fits
core.p: Spec point 2.10B has a B in its number, which means it is examined in **GCSE Biology (separate science) only**, not in Combined Science. You must be able to **describe the structures and functions of the brain**, including the **cerebellum**, the **cerebral hemispheres** and the **medulla oblongata**.
bullets: You need to be able to **identify** each of the three regions on a diagram of the brain.
You need to **state the functions** of each region using the correct key words.
You need to **apply** this: given a symptom, suggest which region is damaged; given a damaged region, predict the effects.
How the brain is investigated with scanners, and why it is hard to treat, are separate spec points and are not covered here.

core.h: The brain as part of the central nervous system
core.p: The **central nervous system (CNS)** is made up of the **brain** and the **spinal cord**. The brain is the coordination centre for almost everything the body does. It receives information from receptors, processes it, and sends out impulses to effectors (muscles and glands).
bullets: The brain is made of **billions of neurones** (nerve cells) that are connected to each other at synapses.
Neurones carry information as **electrical impulses**. The huge number of connections lets the brain process information and control complex behaviour.
The brain is soft and delicate, and is protected inside the **skull**.
The brain is connected to the rest of the body through the **spinal cord**, which runs down inside the backbone.
Different regions of the brain are responsible for different functions. Because of this, damage to one region affects particular abilities and leaves others unchanged.

callouts.p: The brain and the spinal cord.
The brain controls complex behaviour because it contains billions of interconnected neurones arranged in regions that carry out different functions.

core.p: The **cerebrum** is by far the largest part of the brain. It is at the top and front, and it is divided down the middle into two halves called the **cerebral hemispheres**: the left hemisphere and the right hemisphere.
bullets: The outer layer of the cerebral hemispheres is called the **cerebral cortex**.
The surface is **highly folded**. Folding gives a very large surface area, so far more neurones fit inside the skull.
The two hemispheres are joined to each other by nerve fibres, so they can share information.
The **right** cerebral hemisphere controls the muscles on the **left** side of the body.
The **left** cerebral hemisphere controls the muscles on the **right** side of the body.
This crossing over happens because the neurones cross from one side to the other on their way between the brain and the body.

callouts.p: These two words look alike but are different structures. Cerebrum = the large top part (thinking, senses, voluntary movement). Cerebellum = the smaller part at the back and base (balance and coordination). A misspelling that could be either word will not get the mark.

core.p: The cerebral hemispheres are responsible for the 'higher' functions of the brain: everything you are aware of and everything you choose to do.
bullets: **Voluntary movement:** movements you decide to make, such as picking up a pen. Impulses are sent from the cerebral hemispheres to the muscles.
**The senses:** information from receptors, for example in the eyes and ears, is processed here so that you can see (**vision**) and hear.
**Language:** understanding and producing **speech**.
**Memory** and learning.
**Intelligence**, conscious thought and reasoning.
**Personality** and behaviour.
Different areas within the hemispheres deal with different jobs (for example one area for vision), which is why a stroke in one small area might affect speech only.

callouts.p: For the cerebral hemispheres choose from: voluntary movement, senses (e.g. vision), language/speech, memory, intelligence, personality, conscious thought.

core.p: The **cerebellum** is a smaller, rounded region at the **back of the brain**, underneath the rear of the cerebral hemispheres. Like the cerebrum, its surface is folded.
bullets: It controls **balance** and **posture**.
It **coordinates the timing and fine control of muscle activity**, so that movements are smooth and accurate rather than jerky.
The cerebral hemispheres make the decision to move; the cerebellum makes sure the right muscles contract at the right moment and by the right amount.
It uses information from receptors (for example in the muscles, eyes and ears) to adjust movements while they are happening.
Examples of activities that rely on the cerebellum: walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle, writing, catching a ball.
Damage to the cerebellum causes **loss of balance** and **clumsy, poorly coordinated movements**, but the person can still think and can still decide to move.

callouts.p: Controls balance and posture and coordinates the timing and fine control of muscle activity.

core.h: The medulla oblongata: structure and function
core.p: The **medulla oblongata** is at the base of the brain, where the brain joins the **spinal cord**. It is part of the brain, not part of the spinal cord.
bullets: It controls **unconscious (involuntary) activities**: things that happen automatically without you having to think about them.
It controls **heart rate**.
It controls **breathing rate**.
It is also responsible for some reflexes such as swallowing, sneezing and vomiting.
Because it works automatically, heart rate and breathing continue while you are asleep or unconscious.
The medulla sends nerve impulses to the heart and to the muscles used for breathing to speed them up or slow them down, for example during exercise.
Damage to the medulla oblongata is **life-threatening**, because the heartbeat and breathing may stop.

callouts.p: Controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.
Write 'controls heart rate and breathing rate'. Avoid vague answers such as 'controls the heart' or 'controls the lungs'.

core.p: This table is the core of the spec point. If you can reproduce it from memory and find each region on a diagram, you can answer most recall questions.
bullets: Mnemonic for position: the cere**bell**um hangs at the back like a bell; the **med**ulla is in the **mid**line at the bottom, leading to the spinal cord.
Mnemonic for function: cere**b**ellum = **b**alance; **m**edulla = **m**aintains heartbeat and breathing.

core.p: A useful way to organise the three regions is to ask whether you are aware of, and can choose, the activity being controlled.
bullets: **Voluntary (conscious)** actions are ones you decide to carry out. They are started by the **cerebral hemispheres**.
**Involuntary (unconscious)** activities happen automatically. Heart rate and breathing rate are controlled by the **medulla oblongata**.
The **cerebellum** works without you being aware of it, but it acts on voluntary movements, fine-tuning them.
Why is automatic control an advantage? Vital processes carry on without relying on attention, and they continue during sleep.
You can deliberately hold your breath for a short time (cerebral hemispheres), but the medulla's automatic control takes over again and makes you breathe.

head: Activity
Region mainly responsible
Conscious?
rows: Staying upright and timing the kick

core.h: Working together: one action, three regions
core.p: The regions do not work in isolation. Think about running for a bus. Each region contributes something different at the same time.
bullets: **Cerebral hemispheres:** you see the bus (vision), remember that it is the right one (memory), decide to run and send impulses to your leg muscles (voluntary movement).
**Cerebellum:** keeps you balanced and coordinates the timing of the contractions of your leg and arm muscles so that you run smoothly without falling.
**Medulla oblongata:** increases your heart rate and breathing rate so that more oxygen reaches your muscles for respiration.
**Spinal cord:** carries the impulses between the brain and the rest of the body.

core.p: Application questions describe an injury, tumour or stroke and ask you to link it to symptoms. The method is always the same: match the lost function to the region that controls it.
bullets: Problems with **memory, speech, vision, personality** or being unable to make a voluntary movement point to the **cerebral hemispheres**.
Weakness or paralysis on the **left** side of the body points to damage in the **right** cerebral hemisphere, and the other way round.
**Loss of balance**, shaky or clumsy movements and difficulty with precise tasks point to the **cerebellum**.
Abnormal **heart rate or breathing** points to the **medulla oblongata**.
Always finish the link: name the region AND state the normal function that has been lost.

callouts.p: If a question gives symptoms, quote them. 'The patient cannot walk in a straight line, so the cerebellum is damaged, because the cerebellum controls balance and coordination.'

core.p: Edexcel questions commonly show a section through the brain, seen from the side, with label lines. Use size and position to identify each region.
bullets: The **largest** region, filling the top of the diagram and drawn with many folds, is the **cerebrum / cerebral hemisphere**.
The smaller, rounded, finely lined region tucked under the back of the cerebrum is the **cerebellum**.
The stalk-like region at the bottom, leading down out of the brain, is the **medulla oblongata**; it continues downwards as the **spinal cord**.
In a side view you only see one cerebral hemisphere; a view from above shows both the left and right hemispheres.
Spell the names carefully: cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla oblongata.

analogy.p: Think of the brain as a football club. The **cerebral hemispheres** are the manager and the players' decision-making: they watch the game (senses), remember tactics (memory), talk to each other (language) and choose when to pass or shoot (voluntary movement). The **cerebellum** is the coaching that turns a decision into a smooth, well-timed, balanced kick. The **medulla oblongata** is the ground staff who keep the lights and water running all the time without anyone asking (heart rate and breathing rate). If the ground staff stop, the match stops immediately, which is why medulla damage is life-threatening. Where it breaks down: in a club these are separate people who can swap jobs, but brain regions are fixed groups of connected neurones that cannot simply take over each other's work, and they are all communicating constantly through nerve impulses.

terms.d: The brain and the spinal cord.
The organ of the CNS, made of billions of interconnected neurones, that coordinates the body's activities; protected by the skull.
A nerve cell, specialised to carry electrical impulses.
The largest part of the brain, divided into the two cerebral hemispheres.
The left and right halves of the cerebrum; responsible for voluntary movement, senses, language, memory, intelligence and personality.
The highly folded outer layer of the cerebral hemispheres.
The region at the back of the brain that controls balance and posture and coordinates the timing and fine control of muscle activity.
The region at the base of the brain, joining the spinal cord, that controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.
The part of the CNS that runs down inside the backbone and carries impulses between the brain and the rest of the body.
An action that is under conscious control; you choose to do it.
An activity that happens automatically without conscious thought, such as the control of heart rate.
Making muscles work together at the right time and with the right force to give smooth, accurate movement.
The position in which the body is held; maintained by the cerebellum.
The number of heart beats per minute; controlled by the medulla oblongata.
The number of breaths per minute; controlled by the medulla oblongata.

mistakes.w: The cerebellum controls memory and thinking.
mistakes.r: That is the cerebrum (cerebral hemispheres). The cerebellum controls balance, posture and the coordination of muscle activity.

mistakes.w: The cerebellum controls movement.
mistakes.r: Too vague. The cerebral hemispheres start voluntary movements; the cerebellum coordinates the timing and fine control of muscle activity and controls balance.

mistakes.w: The medulla controls the heart and lungs.
mistakes.r: Be precise: the medulla oblongata controls heart rate and breathing rate (unconscious activities).

mistakes.w: The left hemisphere controls the left side of the body.
mistakes.r: Each hemisphere controls the opposite side: the left cerebral hemisphere controls muscles on the right side of the body.

mistakes.w: The medulla is part of the spinal cord.
mistakes.r: The medulla oblongata is part of the brain; it is the region at the base that connects the brain to the spinal cord.

mistakes.w: The medulla controls reflexes such as moving your hand away from a hot object.
mistakes.r: Withdrawal reflexes are coordinated through the spinal cord. For the medulla, give heart rate and breathing rate.

mistakes.w: The brain is one organ so damage anywhere causes the same symptoms.
mistakes.r: Different regions have different functions, so the symptoms depend on which region is damaged.

mistakes.w: The cerebral hemispheres control breathing because you can hold your breath.
mistakes.r: Normal breathing rate is controlled automatically by the medulla oblongata; conscious control is only temporary.

exam.q: Name the part of the brain that controls heart rate.
model: Medulla oblongata
exam.tip: 'Medulla' is normally accepted, but learn the full name.

exam.q: State one function of the cerebellum.
model: Controls balance / posture / coordinates (timing and fine control of) muscle activity
exam.tip: 'Movement' alone is not enough; say balance or coordination.

exam.q: State two functions of the cerebral hemispheres.
model: Any two from: voluntary movement / senses, e.g. vision / language or speech / memory / intelligence / personality / conscious thought
second correct function from the list
exam.tip: Two different functions; do not give 'thinking' and 'thought' as two separate answers.

exam.q: Name the two parts of the central nervous system.
model: Brain and spinal cord
exam.tip: Both are needed for the one mark.

exam.q: Describe the functions of the medulla oblongata.
model: Controls unconscious / involuntary activities
such as heart rate and breathing rate
exam.tip: State the general idea (unconscious) and give the examples.

exam.q: A patient has a tumour in the cerebellum. Describe the effects this could have on the patient.
model: Loss of / poor balance or posture
poor coordination of muscles / jerky or clumsy movements / difficulty with fine movements
exam.tip: Turn each function of the cerebellum into the matching symptom.

exam.q: After a stroke, a person cannot move their left arm. Explain which part of the brain has been damaged.
model: The right cerebral hemisphere
because the cerebral hemispheres control voluntary movement and the right hemisphere controls the muscles on the left side of the body
exam.tip: Opposite sides: left body, right hemisphere.

exam.q: Explain why severe damage to the medulla oblongata is more likely to cause death than damage to the cerebellum.
model: The medulla oblongata controls heart rate and breathing rate
if these stop, oxygen is no longer supplied to cells (for respiration) so the person dies
the cerebellum controls balance and coordination, which are not needed to stay alive
exam.tip: Compare: say something about both regions.

exam.q: Describe how the structure of the cerebral hemispheres allows them to carry out complex functions.
model: They contain billions of (interconnected) neurones
the outer layer / cortex is highly folded, giving a large surface area so more neurones fit in
exam.tip: Structure questions want features you could see or count, each linked to what it allows.

exam.q: A gymnast performs a routine on a balance beam while her heart rate increases. She has learned the routine by practising. Explain the roles of the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum and medulla oblongata during the routine.
model: Cerebral hemispheres: memory is used to recall the routine she has learned
Cerebral hemispheres: control voluntary movement, sending impulses to muscles to start each move
Cerebral hemispheres: process information from the senses, e.g. vision, so she can see the beam
Cerebellum: controls balance and posture so she stays on the beam
Cerebellum: coordinates the timing and fine control of muscle activity so movements are smooth and precise
Medulla oblongata: controls unconscious activities, increasing heart rate and breathing rate
so more oxygen is delivered to muscles for respiration
exam.tip: Levels-marked: cover all three regions and tie each function to something in the routine.

exam.q: Give one difference between the activities controlled by the cerebral hemispheres and those controlled by the medulla oblongata.
model: The cerebral hemispheres control voluntary / conscious activities whereas the medulla oblongata controls involuntary / unconscious activities
exam.tip: Use 'whereas' and mention both regions.

worked.q: A cyclist falls and hits the back of his head. Afterwards he can speak normally and remember the accident, and his pulse and breathing are normal, but he staggers when he walks and cannot do up his buttons. Suggest which region of the brain is damaged and explain your answer. (3 marks)
steps: List what still works: speech and memory (cerebral hemispheres), heart rate and breathing rate (medulla oblongata).
List what has gone wrong: staggering = poor balance; cannot do up buttons = poor fine control of muscles.
Match the lost functions to a region: balance and fine coordination are controlled by the cerebellum.
Check position: the cerebellum is at the back of the brain, which fits a blow to the back of the head.
worked.ans: The cerebellum. It controls balance and coordinates the timing and fine control of muscle activity, and these are the functions he has lost. The cerebral hemispheres and medulla oblongata are unaffected because speech, memory, heart rate and breathing rate are normal.

worked.q: A scan shows a blood clot in the left cerebral hemisphere of a patient. Predict two possible effects on the patient and explain each one. (4 marks)
steps: Recall what the cerebral hemispheres do: voluntary movement, senses, language, memory, intelligence, personality.
Recall the crossing-over rule: the left hemisphere controls muscles on the right side of the body.
Effect 1: weakness or loss of voluntary movement on the right side of the body.
Effect 2: choose another cerebral function, for example difficulty with speech or memory loss.
Give the reason for each effect by stating the normal function.
worked.ans: The patient may be unable to move muscles on the right side of the body, because the left cerebral hemisphere controls voluntary movement on the right side. The patient may also have problems with speech (or memory, or vision), because the cerebral hemispheres are responsible for language (or memory, or the senses).

worked.q: Explain why a person who is in a deep sleep continues to breathe but does not walk about. (2 marks)
steps: Breathing rate is an unconscious activity controlled by the medulla oblongata, which works automatically.
Walking is a voluntary movement started by the cerebral hemispheres, which requires conscious control.
Put the two ideas into one comparison.
worked.ans: Breathing rate is controlled unconsciously by the medulla oblongata, so it continues automatically during sleep. Walking is a voluntary movement controlled by the cerebral hemispheres, so it needs conscious decisions that are not being made while asleep.

bio_edx.1.9.summary: The nervous system carries information as **electrical impulses** along nerve cells called **neurones**. Sensory receptors detect a stimulus, **sensory neurones** carry impulses to the central nervous system (CNS), **relay neurones** pass them on inside the CNS and **motor neurones** carry impulses out to effectors. Neurones are adapted by having an axon, a dendron or dendrites and a myelin sheath, and they pass the signal to each other across tiny gaps called **synapses** using chemicals called **neurotransmitters**.

core.h: The big picture: from stimulus to response
core.p: The nervous system lets the body detect changes and respond to them quickly. A change in the environment is called a **stimulus**. Information about the stimulus travels as electrical impulses along a fixed route of neurones to the central nervous system and back out to the part of the body that responds.
bullets: The **central nervous system (CNS)** is the **brain and spinal cord**. It coordinates the response.
The route is: stimulus -> receptor -> sensory neurone -> CNS (relay neurone) -> motor neurone -> effector -> response.
An **effector** is a muscle or a gland. Muscles respond by contracting; glands respond by releasing (secreting) a substance such as a hormone or an enzyme.
Nerves you can see in a dissection are bundles of many neurones.
Nervous communication is fast and short-lived because the signal is electrical along each neurone.

callouts.p: A change in the internal or external environment that is detected by receptors.
Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector. Examiners often ask you to put these in order or to name the missing one.

core.p: **Sensory receptors** are cells that detect a stimulus. When a receptor cell is stimulated it starts (generates) an electrical impulse in a sensory neurone. Each type of receptor detects one kind of stimulus only.
bullets: Receptor cells are often grouped together in **sense organs**, for example the eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin.
Receptor cells in the retina of the eye detect light.
Receptor cells in the skin detect touch, pressure, pain and temperature change.
Receptor cells in the ear detect sound; receptors in the nose and on the tongue detect chemicals.
The receptor does not carry the impulse to the CNS itself: it passes the information on to the **sensory neurone**.

head: Sense organ
Stimulus detected by its receptor cells

callouts.t: Receptor is not the same as sense organ
callouts.p: The eye is a sense organ. The receptors are the light-sensitive cells in its retina. If a question asks for the receptor, name the cells or say 'receptor cells in the ...'.

core.p: A neurone is a specialised cell adapted to carry electrical impulses from one place to another. All three types have the same basic parts, but arranged differently.
bullets: **Cell body**: contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm and other sub-cellular structures.
**Dendrites**: fine branches that receive impulses from receptor cells or from other neurones. Lots of branches mean a neurone can connect with many other neurones.
**Dendron**: a long extension that carries impulses **towards** the cell body.
**Axon**: a long extension that carries impulses **away from** the cell body.
**Axon terminals**: the branched endings of the axon, where the neurone passes the signal on to the next cell.
**Myelin sheath**: a fatty layer wrapped around the axon or dendron of many neurones.

callouts.p: Axon: carries impulses away from the cell body. Dendron: carries impulses towards the cell body.
Axon = Away from the cell body.

core.h: Why neurones are long, and why they have a myelin sheath
core.p: Exam questions on this spec point usually ask you to **explain how the structure of a neurone is related to its function**. Always link a named structure to what it does and why that helps.
bullets: Neurones are **long** (the axon or dendron can be over a metre) so that one cell can carry an impulse a long distance. Fewer cells in the route means fewer synapses, and each synapse slows the signal down.
The **myelin sheath** is an **electrical insulator**. It stops the impulse leaking away or passing sideways into neighbouring neurones.
The myelin sheath **speeds up** the transmission of the impulse. There are gaps in the sheath and the impulse 'jumps' from one gap to the next instead of travelling along every bit of the axon.
**Dendrites and axon terminals are branched** so the neurone can receive impulses from, and pass impulses to, many other cells.
Faster impulses mean faster responses, which helps an animal avoid danger and coordinate movement.

callouts.t: Two jobs of the myelin sheath
callouts.p: It insulates the neurone AND it speeds up the transmission of electrical impulses. Give both for two marks.
Do not write that the myelin sheath keeps the neurone warm or protects it. It is an electrical insulator.

core.p: A **sensory neurone** carries electrical impulses from receptor cells to the central nervous system.
bullets: Receptor cells are at one end, joined to the neurone by dendrites.
A **long dendron** carries the impulse from the receptor cells towards the cell body.
The **cell body** is part-way along the neurone, off to one side, not at the end.
A (usually shorter) **axon** carries the impulse from the cell body to the CNS.
Axon terminals inside the CNS pass the signal to a relay neurone.
Both dendron and axon have a myelin sheath.

callouts.p: If the cell body is in the middle of the neurone, sitting on a side branch, it is a sensory neurone.

core.p: A **relay neurone** is found only **inside the CNS** (brain and spinal cord). It links sensory neurones to motor neurones.
bullets: It is short, because it only has to carry the impulse a small distance within the CNS.
Many short **dendrites** carry impulses from sensory neurones to the cell body.
An **axon** carries impulses from the cell body to motor neurones.
Because relay neurones connect with many other neurones, they allow the CNS to coordinate the response.
In exam diagrams it is the small neurone drawn inside the spinal cord.

core.p: A **motor neurone** carries electrical impulses from the central nervous system to an effector (a muscle or a gland).
bullets: The **cell body is at one end**, inside the CNS.
Many short **dendrites** on the cell body receive impulses from relay neurones (or other neurones) in the CNS.
One **long axon** carries the impulse from the cell body to the effector.
The axon has a **myelin sheath** to insulate it and speed up the impulse.
**Axon terminals** at the far end pass the signal to the effector cells, for example muscle cells, which then contract.

head: Feature
Sensory neurone
Relay neurone
Motor neurone
rows: Part-way along, on a side branch
Within the CNS, among the dendrites
At one end, in the CNS

callouts.p: Sensory = towards the CNS. Motor = away from the CNS to an effector. Writing 'motor neurones carry impulses to the brain' scores nothing.

core.p: Neurones do not actually touch each other. Where two neurones meet there is a tiny gap called a **synapse**. The electrical impulse cannot cross the gap, so the signal is carried across by a chemical instead.
bullets: The chemical is called a **neurotransmitter**.
The neurone bringing the impulse ends in an **axon terminal**. This is where neurotransmitter is released.
The membrane of the next neurone has **receptors** that the neurotransmitter fits (binds to).
There are also synapses between motor neurones and effector cells.
So transmission is **electrical along a neurone** but **chemical across a synapse**.

callouts.p: The gap between two neurones, where the signal is transmitted by a neurotransmitter.
A chemical released from the axon terminal of one neurone that diffuses across the synapse and causes a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

core.h: How an impulse crosses a synapse, step by step
core.p: This sequence is a favourite 3 or 4 mark question. Learn the steps in order and use the words release, diffuse, bind and new impulse.
bullets: 1. An electrical impulse travels along the axon and **arrives at the axon terminal** of the first neurone.
2. This causes the **neurotransmitter to be released** into the gap.
3. The neurotransmitter **diffuses across the gap** (from where it is in high concentration to where it is in low concentration).
4. The neurotransmitter **binds to receptors** on the membrane of the next neurone.
5. This **generates (triggers) a new electrical impulse** in the next neurone.
The neurotransmitter is then removed from the gap, so the next neurone is not stimulated over and over again by one impulse.

callouts.t: The impulse does not jump the gap
callouts.p: Never write that the impulse, the electricity or the signal 'jumps' or 'diffuses' across the synapse. The NEUROTRANSMITTER diffuses across; a NEW impulse starts in the next neurone.

core.h: Consequences of synapses: one direction and a delay
core.p: Because the signal has to change from electrical to chemical and back again, synapses affect how impulses travel. Higher-mark questions ask you to explain these effects.
bullets: **One direction only**: neurotransmitter is released only from the axon terminal, and the receptors for it are only on the next neurone. So the signal can only pass from the first neurone to the second, never backwards.
**Slower transmission**: diffusion of the neurotransmitter across the gap takes time, so each synapse delays the signal slightly.
This is why a pathway with fewer synapses gives a faster response.
**Connections**: one neurone can form synapses with many others, so impulses can be passed on along different routes and the CNS can coordinate complicated responses.
Many drugs and poisons act at synapses, for example by blocking the receptors so that the neurotransmitter cannot bind and no new impulse is generated.

callouts.p: Along a neurone: electrical impulse (fast). Across a synapse: diffusion of a chemical neurotransmitter (slower).

core.h: Calculating the speed of an impulse
core.p: You may be given data about how far and how fast impulses travel. Use speed = distance / time and take care with units.
bullets: speed (m/s) = distance (m) / time (s).
Convert millimetres to metres by dividing by 1000, and centimetres to metres by dividing by 100.
Convert milliseconds (ms) to seconds by dividing by 1000.
Neurones with a myelin sheath conduct impulses much faster than neurones without one.
If a route includes synapses, the total time is longer than the neurone speed alone would predict, because of the delay at each synapse.

callouts.p: Write the equation, substitute, then give the answer with its unit. A correct method with a slip in arithmetic still earns marks.

core.p: The command word is usually **explain**, so every structure you name must be linked to a reason. A simple pattern works: structure, what it does, why that helps.
bullets: Long axon -> carries impulses over a long distance -> to reach an effector far from the CNS.
Myelin sheath -> insulates the axon -> so impulses are transmitted faster.
Many dendrites -> connect with many other neurones -> so impulses can be received from several places.
Axon terminals containing neurotransmitter -> release it into the synapse -> so the signal passes to the next cell.
Always say **electrical impulse**, not 'message' or 'signal', when you describe what travels along a neurone.

callouts.p: Mark schemes credit: electrical impulse, axon, dendron, dendrites, myelin sheath, insulates, neurotransmitter, diffuses, receptors, effector.

analogy.t: A relay race with a river in the way
analogy.p: Each neurone is a runner sprinting along their own stretch of track: that is the fast electrical impulse. Between two runners there is a river with no bridge (the synapse). The runner cannot cross, so they throw a ball over (the neurotransmitter). When the next runner catches it (it binds to receptors), they set off on their own sprint (a new impulse). Only the first runner has balls and only the second has a catching glove, so the race can only go one way, and the throw takes extra time. Where it breaks down: nothing physical travels along a neurone the way a runner moves along a track, the neurotransmitter spreads out by diffusion rather than being aimed, and one real neurone can pass its signal to many others at once.

terms.d: A nerve cell, specialised to transmit electrical impulses.
The electrical signal that travels along a neurone.
A change in the environment that is detected by receptors.
A cell that detects a stimulus and generates an electrical impulse in a sensory neurone.
The brain and spinal cord; it coordinates responses.
A neurone that carries impulses from receptor cells to the CNS.
A short neurone inside the CNS that carries impulses from sensory neurones to motor neurones.
A neurone that carries impulses from the CNS to an effector.
A muscle or gland that brings about a response.
The part of a neurone that contains the nucleus.
The long extension of a neurone that carries impulses away from the cell body.
The long extension of a neurone that carries impulses towards the cell body.
Fine branches that receive impulses from receptor cells or other neurones.
A fatty layer around an axon or dendron that insulates it electrically and speeds up impulse transmission.
The gap between two neurones, across which the signal is passed by a neurotransmitter.
A chemical released at an axon terminal that diffuses across a synapse and triggers a new impulse in the next neurone.
The end of an axon, where neurotransmitter is released.

mistakes.w: The electrical impulse jumps across the synapse.
mistakes.r: The impulse cannot cross. A neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap, binds to receptors and a new impulse is generated in the next neurone.

mistakes.w: Neurones carry messages or signals.
mistakes.r: Say electrical impulses. 'Messages' is too vague to gain the mark.

mistakes.w: Motor neurones carry impulses from receptors to the brain.
mistakes.r: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

mistakes.w: The myelin sheath protects the neurone or keeps it warm.
mistakes.r: The myelin sheath is an electrical insulator and speeds up the transmission of impulses.

mistakes.w: The axon carries impulses towards the cell body.
mistakes.r: The axon carries impulses away from the cell body. The dendron (and dendrites) carry impulses towards it.

mistakes.w: The neurotransmitter moves across by active transport or just 'moves' across.
mistakes.r: It diffuses across the gap. Use the word diffuses.

mistakes.w: Relay neurones are found in the arm or in muscles.
mistakes.r: Relay neurones are found only in the CNS: the brain and spinal cord.

mistakes.w: The receptor is the eye or the skin.
mistakes.r: Those are sense organs. The receptors are the receptor cells inside them that detect the stimulus.

mistakes.w: Synapses speed up the impulse.
mistakes.r: Synapses slow transmission down, because diffusion of the neurotransmitter takes time.

exam.q: State the function of a sensory neurone.
model: Carries (electrical) impulses from receptor cells to the central nervous system / brain / spinal cord.
exam.tip: Give both ends of the journey: from where and to where.

exam.q: Name the gap between two neurones.
model: Synapse.
exam.tip: A one-word answer is enough for 'name'.

exam.q: Which part of a neurone carries impulses away from the cell body?
model: Axon.
exam.tip: Axon = away.

exam.q: Describe the function of the myelin sheath.
model: It insulates the neurone / axon (electrically).
It speeds up the transmission of the (electrical) impulse.
exam.tip: Two marks, two different points: insulation and speed.

exam.q: Describe two differences between the structure of a sensory neurone and a motor neurone.
model: The cell body of a sensory neurone is part-way along the neurone, but in a motor neurone it is at one end.
A sensory neurone has a long dendron (and a shorter axon), but a motor neurone has short dendrites and a long axon.
exam.tip: A difference needs both sides: say what each neurone has.

exam.q: Describe how an impulse is transmitted across a synapse.
model: Neurotransmitter is released (from the axon terminal) when the impulse arrives.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap / synapse.
It binds to receptors on the next neurone and a new (electrical) impulse is generated.
exam.tip: Release, diffuse, bind, new impulse. Never say the impulse crosses.

exam.q: Explain why impulses can travel in only one direction across a synapse.
model: Neurotransmitter is only released from the axon terminal of the first neurone.
Receptors for the neurotransmitter are only on the (membrane of the) next neurone.
exam.tip: Think about where the chemical is made and where it can be detected.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of a motor neurone is related to its function.
model: It has a long axon so impulses can be carried a long distance from the CNS to the effector.
The axon has a myelin sheath which insulates it, so impulses are transmitted faster.
It has many dendrites so it can receive impulses from other / relay neurones.
It has axon terminals that release neurotransmitter to pass the signal to the effector / muscle cells.
exam.tip: Each mark is a structure linked to a reason. A list of parts without reasons scores poorly.

exam.q: A drug blocks the receptors on the neurone after a synapse. Explain the effect this has on the transmission of impulses.
model: The neurotransmitter is still released and diffuses across the gap.
It cannot bind to the receptors because they are blocked.
So no new impulse is generated in the next neurone / the impulse is not passed on.
exam.tip: Work through the normal steps and say exactly which one is stopped.

exam.q: An impulse travels 0.9 m along a neurone in 0.012 s. Calculate the speed of the impulse.
model: speed = distance / time = 0.9 / 0.012
exam.tip: Write the substitution line: it earns the method mark.

exam.q: When a person touches a sharp object, receptor cells in the skin are stimulated and a muscle in the arm contracts. Describe how the information travels from the receptor cells to the muscle, including how it passes from one neurone to the next.
model: Receptor cells in the skin detect the stimulus and generate an electrical impulse.
The impulse travels along a sensory neurone (dendron then axon) to the CNS / spinal cord.
At the synapse a neurotransmitter is released from the axon terminal.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap and binds to receptors on the relay neurone, generating a new impulse.
The impulse passes along the relay neurone and across another synapse to a motor neurone.
The motor neurone carries the impulse along its axon to the effector / muscle, which contracts.
exam.tip: A 6 mark answer needs a logical order and correct terms. Follow the route and include the synapse steps once in detail.

worked.q: A motor neurone running from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot is 1.2 m long. An impulse takes 15 ms to travel along it. Calculate the speed of the impulse in m/s.
steps: Convert the time to seconds: 15 ms = 15 / 1000 = 0.015 s.
Write the equation: speed = distance / time.
Substitute: speed = 1.2 / 0.015.

worked.q: An impulse travels along a route 0.50 m long at 50 m/s. The route includes two synapses, and each synapse adds a delay of 0.001 s. Calculate the total time taken.
steps: Time along the neurones = distance / speed = 0.50 / 50 = 0.010 s.
Delay at synapses = 2 x 0.001 = 0.002 s.
Comment: the synapses make up a noticeable part of the total time, which is why routes with fewer synapses give faster responses.

worked.q: A diagram shows a neurone with its cell body on a short side branch half-way along, a receptor cell at one end and endings in the spinal cord at the other. Identify the type of neurone and explain your answer.
steps: Look at the cell body: it is part-way along, not at one end, which is the pattern for a sensory neurone.
Look at what each end connects to: receptor cells at one end and the CNS (spinal cord) at the other.
A neurone carrying impulses from receptor cells to the CNS is a sensory neurone.
The part from the receptor to the cell body is the dendron; the part from the cell body to the CNS is the axon.
worked.ans: It is a sensory neurone, because its cell body is part-way along and it carries impulses from receptor cells to the CNS.

svg.cap: A synapse. When an impulse arrives at the axon terminal, neurotransmitter stored in vesicles is released into the gap. It diffuses across and binds to receptors on the next neurone, where a new electrical impulse is generated. Transmission is one-way because only the axon terminal releases neurotransmitter and only the next neurone has the receptors.
